time_scope: modern descriptive/lexical data; Milner 1966 root sample analyzed 2013
claim: Samoan syllables generally fit (C)V1(V2): codas are prohibited, onsets are simplex and optional, and a second vowel may occupy a bimoraic nucleus.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: VV syllabification is partly analytically unresolved; certain VV sequences can be heterosyllabic in special contexts.

claim: The VV sequences /ei eu ai au ou oi ui/ are treated as tautosyllabic diphthongs; other unlike-vowel sequences are treated as heterosyllabic in the authors' working analysis.
normalized_environment: VV -> tautosyllabic iff {ei,eu,ai,au,ou,oi,ui} under adopted analysis
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The authors explicitly acknowledge unresolved issues, especially identical-vowel sequences and special contexts where apparent diphthongs behave heterosyllabically.

claim: Primary stress falls on the final syllable when its nucleus is bimoraic; otherwise stress falls on the penultimate syllable.
normalized_environment: final heavy -> final stress; else penultimate stress
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Morpheme-boundary and idiolectal patterns can exhibit strict penultimate-mora behavior instead.

claim: Across some morpheme boundaries, stress can follow a strict penultimate-mora pattern rather than the ordinary diphthong-based syllable parse, as in /fe+ita/ -> feíta.
normalized_environment: strict penultimate-mora stress in special morphological contexts
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The authors treat these as special contexts and do not generalize the pattern to all words.

claim: The literary inventory lacks native /k r h/ but these consonants occur in loans; /h/ is reported word-initially in most loan cases.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Colloquial tautala leaga has /k/ as the merger outcome of /t,k/ and /r/ from loans merges with /l/.

claim: Tautala leaga is characterized by three phoneme mergers relative to the literary register: t~k -> k, n~ŋ -> ŋ, and loan r~l -> l.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The paper's quantitative root phonotactics focus on tautala lelei rather than this colloquial system.

claim: The root list was constrained by a canonical-root criterion of no more than four moras, used to screen likely morphologically complex entries.
scope: corpus construction informed by prior Samoan descriptions
exceptions_or_counterexamples: This is an operational/canonical-root criterion for the dataset, not demonstrated as an exceptionless grammatical maximum.

claim: Medial syllables in tri- and quadrisyllabic roots are overwhelmingly CV with a short vowel: Table 2 gives medial counts CV=295, CVV=3, V=69, VV=0.
formal_environment: non-initial, non-final syllable in 3-4 syllable roots
normalized_environment: medial σ strongly favors short monomoraic V; VV absent in sample
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Three medial CVV tokens occur; therefore long/diphthongal medial nuclei are very rare rather than categorically impossible.

claim: Bilabial /p m/ show a strong initial-position preference, while non-labial sonorants /n l ŋ/ are much more frequent non-initially.
scope: type-token counts of consonant occurrences in root list
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Labiodentals /f v/ do not share the bilabial initial preference; the authors stress that this is a distributional bias, not a categorical ban.

claim: The clearest CV gap is a nearly categorical avoidance of /v/ before back vowels: Table 7 has /vo/=2 and /vu/=0.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The restriction is nearly categorical rather than absolute because /vo/ is attested twice; /va/ is frequent.

claim: Diphthongs are rare relative to short vowels and are dominated by /ai au/; /ui/ occurs 17 times, with 7 cases word-initial, where Mosel & Hovdhaugen report an initial glide realization that complicates diphthong status.
normalized_environment: diphthongs rare; /aI,aU/ especially frequent; initial ui analytically qualified
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Initial /ui/ may be realized with an initial glide, so some tokens may not be straightforward phonetic diphthongs.
